analysis.one_liner: Replaces the income and estate taxes with a national sales tax and a business tax.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: introduced in October 2005 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, it died without a hearing or vote when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the federal income tax — including capital gains taxes and the alternative minimum tax — along with the estate, gift, and corporate income taxes, and shut down the IRS by cutting its funding after 2010. In their place it would impose an 8.4% national sales tax on goods and services, an 8.4% tax on business gross profits, and an 8.4% tax on imports, with states collecting the sales tax. It includes a monthly rebate covering the sales tax up to the poverty level for registered families, plus a savings-account program for low-income individuals.
analysis.who_benefits: The highest earners and holders of large estates gain the most: they would stop paying income, capital gains, and estate taxes entirely. Because a sales tax falls on what people spend rather than what they earn — and wealthier households save a larger share of their income — the burden of raising the same money shifts toward families who spend most of each paycheck. The poverty-level rebate softens the blow for the lowest-income families but does not extend above the poverty line.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the income tax, capital gains tax, alternative minimum tax, and estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes [S2][S3].
Repeals the corporate income tax and replaces it with an 8.4% tax on business gross profits, plus an 8.4% tax on the customs value of imports [S2].
Ends IRS operations by prohibiting funding of the Internal Revenue Service after fiscal year 2010 [S2].
Provides a monthly 'family consumption allowance' rebate to registered families, equal to the sales tax on the federal poverty level, paid through the Social Security Administration [S3].

Includes the Savings for Working Families Act, letting low-income individuals build individual development accounts for education, a first home, or a business, with federal matching funds routed to financial institutions [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Households that spend most of their income — wage earners, retirees drawing down savings — would pay the new 8.4% tax on nearly everything they buy, on top of the Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes the bill leaves untouched. Families would also have to register annually to receive the rebate, and states would take on the cost of collecting a federal tax.

drawbacks.text: A consumption tax is regressive relative to the income tax it replaces: the richest households, which save much of their income and would no longer pay capital gains or estate taxes, gain the most, while families living paycheck to paycheck pay the 8.4% rate on nearly all of it [S3].
The rebate only covers the tax up to the poverty level, so families earning above it absorb the full rate on every additional dollar they spend [S3].

An 8.4% rate on consumption and business gross profits is far below the rates other national sales tax proposals used when claiming to replace income tax revenue, so the plan as written would very likely not raise what the repealed taxes did — a gap that would eventually have to be closed by raising the rate, cutting spending, or borrowing.
The bill also repeals the public financing provisions for presidential elections, ending the voluntary checkoff that funds major-party nominees' general election campaigns [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a large, permanent tax cut to the top of the income distribution — no income tax, no capital gains tax, no estate tax — while converting the main federal revenue source into a flat tax on spending. The family rebate and the savings-account program are real benefits for low-income households, but they are layered on top of a structure whose net effect is to shift the tax burden from accumulated wealth toward everyday consumption. The unusually low 8.4% rate also raises a basic arithmetic problem that the bill does not solve.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late October 2005, read twice, and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; it died when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim DeMint introduced the bill on October 26, 2005, joined by Sen. Lindsey Graham [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — was ever recorded before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary working households are better off that the bill died, since the existing — more progressive — tax structure remained in place; the estate and income tax repeal that would have gone to the wealthiest households never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Working households kept the current tax code

for.name: Jim DeMint
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to replace the income and estate taxes with a national sales tax and business tax.

for.name: Lindsey Graham
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only additional sponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that never scheduled action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never moved past referral.

industries.note: The bill eliminates income, capital gains, and estate taxes entirely, an enormous benefit concentrated at the top, while replacing the revenue with a flat tax on everyone's spending. The gain to wealth is paid for by households that consume most of their income.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax compliance industry
industries.note: Repealing the income tax would eliminate most individual and corporate tax filing, wiping out a large compliance industry. Consumers would stop paying for tax preparation, but they would pay a new federal tax at the register.

Every seller of taxable goods and services becomes a federal tax collector, compensated with a credit of the greater of $200 or 0.25% of tax remitted. This makes retailers a permanent part of federal tax administration.

The bill taxes financial intermediation services but also routes federal matching funds for low-income savings accounts through financial institutions, giving them a new federally subsidized line of business.
States that run sales taxes would collect the federal tax for a 0.25% administrative fee and gain a formal role in federal tax administration.
